title: Episode 201: Ancient Egypt: Moses, the Ten Plagues, and the Iron Chariots of Pharaoh
description:
During the height of Egypt's Nineteenth Dynasty, a militaristic new pharaoh arose who viewed the burgeoning Hebrew population of the Nile Delta as a dangerous fifth column. Enslaving hundreds of thousands of Israelites to manufacture mud bricks for the monumental treasure cities of Pithom and Pi-Ramses, Pharaoh decreed that every newborn Hebrew boy be cast into the Nile. Hidden in a waterproof papyrus basket among the reeds, an infant named Moses was discovered and adopted by Pharaoh's own daughter, raised in the lap of royal luxury before fleeing into the desert of Midian after slaying a cruel Egyptian taskmaster. Summoned by the Voice from the burning bush, Moses returned to face the living god-king of Egypt with a commanding ultimatum: 'Let my people go.' Discover the supernatural clash of the Ten Plagues, the sacred night of Passover, and the cataclysmic parting of the Sea of Reeds.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, we conclude our Ancient Egypt saga with one of the greatest epic narratives in human literature: the Exodus. In the shadow of colossal temples and iron-wheeled war chariots, a shepherd with a wooden staff confronted the mightiest empire on earth. Here is George with the story of the reed basket, the Ten Plagues, and the waters of the Red Sea.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: 'A PHARAOH WHO KNEW NOT JOSEPH'
As the centuries passed in the Nile Delta, the biblical Book of Exodus records a chilling turning point in the fortunes of the Hebrew people: 'Now there arose a new king over Egypt, who knew not Joseph.' Most historical scholars identify this martial era with the Nineteenth Dynasty—the reign of Seti I and his colossal son, Ramses II, known to history as Ramses the Great. The warrior pharaohs, engaged in brutal, protracted wars against the rival Hittite Empire in Syria, looked with mounting paranoia upon the hundreds of thousands of Hebrews living in the strategic borderlands of Goshen. Fearing that in the event of an Asiatic invasion, the Hebrews might join with Egypt's enemies, take up arms against the crown, and flee the country, Pharaoh instituted a system of state-sponsored chattel slavery. Hebrew men were organized into forced labor gangs under the cruel whips of Egyptian taskmasters, toiling in scorching clay pits under the blazing desert sun to dig Nile mud, mix it with chopped straw, and press it into millions of heavy sun-dried bricks. These enslaved multitudes built the monumental delta royal capital of Pi-Ramses and the vast imperial store city of Pithom. Yet despite the crushing oppression and backbreaking labor, the Hebrew population continued to multiply, driving Pharaoh to a decree of savage infanticide: ordering Hebrew midwives Shiphrah and Puah, and then all Egyptian citizens, to seize and drown every newborn Hebrew baby boy in the waters of the Nile.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE REED BASKET ON THE WATER
In the midst of state terror, a Levite woman named Jochebed gave birth to a healthy, beautiful baby boy. For three agonizing months, she hid the crying infant in the shadowed corners of their mud-brick hut. But when concealment became impossible, she took an ark woven from thick papyrus reeds, daubed it with pitch and bitumen to make it completely waterproof, placed the sleeping baby inside, and gently set it among the reeds at the edge of the Nile River, while the child's older sister Miriam stood watch from a distance. That morning, Pharaoh's daughter descended to the sacred riverbank with her maidens to bathe in the cool waters. Spotting the floating basket among the reeds, she ordered her servant to fetch it. Opening the lid, she looked upon the weeping infant and was moved to deep compassion: 'This is one of the Hebrews' children.' Miriam stepped forward with quick, courageous wit, asking the Egyptian princess if she should summon a Hebrew nursemaid. Miriam brought Jochebed, who was paid royal wages to nurse her own child in safety. When the boy grew older, the princess adopted him into the royal palace, naming him Moses—meaning 'drawn from the water.' Raised as an Egyptian prince in the palaces of Pi-Ramses, educated in complex hieroglyphics, military tactics, literature, and court diplomacy, Moses enjoyed every aristocratic privilege, yet his heart remained tied to the suffering and groans of his enslaved brethren.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE BURNING BUSH AT MOUNT HOREB
At age forty, Moses's royal life shattered in an instant. Visiting a construction site, he witnessed an Egyptian taskmaster brutally beating a defenseless Hebrew slave. Glancing about to ensure no royal guards were watching, Moses struck the Egyptian down and buried his body in the desert sand. When the murder became known to Pharaoh the following day, a royal warrant of death was issued. Moses fled across the barren Sinai wilderness to the desert of Midian, near the Gulf of Aqaba. There, the former prince traded his fine linen for a coarse shepherd's robe, married Zipporah, daughter of the Midianite priest Jethro, and spent forty humbling years tending flocks of sheep in the rugged mountain silence, learning patience and survival in the wilderness. Then, while driving his flock near Mount Horeb—the Mountain of God—Moses stopped in wonder: a desert acacia bush was burning with bright, roaring flames, yet the leaves and branches were not consumed. As Moses stepped closer to investigate, a voice of thunder echoed from the flames: 'Moses, Moses! Put off thy shoes from off thy feet, for the place whereon thou standest is holy ground.' God revealed His eternal sacred name: 'I AM THAT I AM.' God declared that He had seen the affliction of His people in Egypt, heard their cry, and commanded the eighty-year-old shepherd to return to the heart of the Egyptian empire, face the divine god-king upon his golden throne, and demand: 'Let My people go, that they may serve Me.'

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE WAR OF THE GODS: THE TEN PLAGUES
Accompanied by his eloquent brother Aaron, Moses walked into the colossal, pillared audience chamber of Pharaoh. Holding a simple wooden shepherd's staff, Moses delivered the divine demand. Pharaoh laughed in cold contempt: 'Who is the Lord, that I should obey His voice to let Israel go? I know not the Lord, neither will I let Israel go!' What followed was not merely an environmental catastrophe, but a direct supernatural war against the entire pantheon of Egyptian deities. When Moses struck the sacred Nile with his staff, the river turned to putrid, clotted blood, killing the fish, polluting the drinking water, and utterly humiliating Hapi, the god of the Nile inundation. Next came plagues of swarming frogs leaping into royal bedchambers and bread ovens, mocking Heqet, the frog-headed goddess of fertility; then swarms of lice from the dust, which Egyptian court magicians could not replicate, crying in panic: 'This is the finger of God!' Plagues of swarming flies, diseased livestock, painful festering boils, and flaming hailstones devastated Egyptian agriculture and shattered the temples of Isis and Osiris. Yet in the Land of Goshen where the Hebrews lived, not a single drop of hail fell or fly buzzed. A supernatural, palpable darkness smothered Egypt for three terrifying days, shutting out every beam of light and utterly humiliating Ra, the supreme sun god of Pharaoh. Yet after every plague, Pharaoh hardened his heart, stubbornly refusing to release his captive workforce.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE PASSOVER NIGHT IN GOSHEN
The divine conflict culminated in a tenth and final judgment of terrifying finality. Moses warned Pharaoh that at midnight, the Lord would pass through the land, and every firstborn in Egypt—from the firstborn of Pharaoh sitting on the throne to the firstborn of the maidservant behind the millstone, and all the firstborn of beasts—would die. To protect their families from the destroyer, the Israelites received exact divine instructions for the very first Passover. Every Hebrew household selected an unblemished yearling male lamb or goat, slaughtered it at twilight on the fourteenth of Nisan, and brushed the fresh blood with a bunch of hyssop onto the two wooden doorposts and upper lintels of their homes. They roasted the meat over fire, eating it in haste with bitter herbs and unleavened bread, with their robes tucked into their belts, sandals strapped on their feet, and walking staffs in hand. At midnight, a great, chilling cry arose throughout all the land of Egypt: there was not a single Egyptian home where someone was not dead, including Pharaoh's own beloved firstborn son and heir. Shattered, weeping, and grieving, Pharaoh summoned Moses and Aaron in the dead of night and screamed: 'Rise up, and get you forth from among my people, both ye and the children of Israel; and go, serve the Lord, as ye have said! Also take your flocks and your herds, as ye have said, and be gone; and bless me also!'

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE WATERS PART AT THE SEA OF REEDS
Before dawn on that historic morning, a vast multitude of six hundred thousand Hebrew men on foot, along with women, children, their flocks, and a vast mixed multitude of sympathizers, marched out of Egypt carrying their dough before it was leavened, guided by a miraculous pillar of cloud by day and a pillar of fire by night. But as the Israelites camped by the shores of the Sea of Reeds—traditionally identified with the Gulf of Suez or the Bitter Lakes—Pharaoh experienced a violent surge of remorse. 'Why have we done this,' he raged to his nobles, 'that we have let Israel go from serving us?' Pharaoh harnessed his royal gold war chariot and mobilized six hundred chosen elite chariots, commanded by the most ruthless officers in the Egyptian empire, pursuing the fleeing slaves with thundering bronze-rimmed wheels. As the choking dust clouds of the approaching Egyptian army darkened the desert horizon, the trapped Israelites cried out in panic to Moses: 'Because there were no graves in Egypt, hast thou taken us away to die in the wilderness?' Moses stood firm on the wind-swept shore, raising his voice above the whistling gale: 'Fear ye not, stand still, and see the salvation of the Lord! The Egyptians whom ye have seen today, ye shall see them again no more forever!' Stretching his wooden staff over the waters, a mighty east wind blew all through the night, driving the sea back and walling the waters like glass on the right hand and on the left. The children of Israel walked through the midst of the sea on dry ground.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE SINKING CHARIOTS AND THE SONG OF MIRIAM
In the pre-dawn darkness of the morning watch, the Egyptian army charged blindly into the parted seabed in hot pursuit. But as the heavy bronze and iron-rimmed chariot wheels rolled across the muddy sea floor, God threw the Egyptian host into wild confusion, twisting and clogging the chariot axles so that they drove with heavy difficulty. The terrified Egyptian officers screamed to one another: 'Let us flee from the face of Israel, for the Lord fighteth for them against the Egyptians!' But it was too late. God commanded Moses: 'Stretch out thine hand over the sea.' Moses stretched forth his staff over the waters. As the morning sun broke across the horizon, the towering walls of water collapsed with a deafening roar, surging back into their natural channels with irresistible hydraulic force. The raging waves engulfed Pharaoh's elite chariots, war horses, and armored horsemen; not a single Egyptian warrior survived the deluge. Standing on the eastern shore of the sea, looking out over the floating bronze shields and chariot wreckage washing ashore in the surf, Miriam the prophetess took a timbrel in her hand. Leading all the women of Israel in sacred dancing and joyous praise, she sang the immortal anthem of liberation: 'Sing ye to the Lord, for He hath triumphed gloriously; the horse and his rider hath He thrown into the sea!' The chains of four centuries of Egyptian bondage were broken forever; Israel was free, marching toward Mount Sinai and the Promised Land.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
The Exodus from Egypt shattered the myth of the divine pharaohs and birthed a free nation bound by a moral covenant with God. But far to the east, along the upper reaches of the Tigris River, a far darker and more terrifying military colossus was beginning to stir. Next week, we enter the brutal realm of The Assyrian Empire with Episode 202: The Iron Wolf of Nineveh: Tiglath-Pileser III, the world's first professional standing army, the psychology of siege terror, and the tragic fall of the Northern Kingdom of Israel. Until then, thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories.
